---
title: "Concepts"
---

tether borrows its shape from [jj](https://jj-vcs.dev): there is a working copy
that gets snapshotted on every command, commits that record it, and `new` to
start working on top of a commit. What differs is *what* is versioned: not
files in a tree, but the state of external systems that keep their own
history.

## The working copy is the manifests

A dataset is a directory holding `tether.toml` and `.tether/objects/<key>.toml`,
one manifest per registered object. A manifest names the object (`kind` +
`locator`), its policy, and -- once committed -- its recorded `state` and, if
any, its `pin`. Committing a dataset means committing those manifests to the
enclosing git/jj repository. History, branching, bookmarks, workspaces, and
sharing are therefore the VCS's, not tether's. What the VCS cannot see -- what
tether did to the *stores* to get there -- goes in tether's own
[operation log](#the-operation-log).

| jj | tether |
| --- | --- |
| working copy | the VCS working dir; the committed thing is the manifests |
| snapshot on every command | **snapshot**: concurrent fan-out fingerprint of every object |
| `jj commit` | **pin** fan-out + write state into manifests + `jj/git commit` |
| `jj new <rev>` | checkout + **fork** fan-out (fresh writable branch per object) |
| stale working copy | manifest hash recorded at fork differs from HEAD: refuse writes |
| `jj diff` | **diff**: object-level manifest diff; `--content` asks each backend for its native diff |
| `jj log` | **log**: an object's *native* history (snapshots / versions / commits); ids feed `add --at` |
| detached head | an object registered `--at` a state that is not a branch head; `commit` pins it, `new` forks from it |
| -- | **verify** (pins still resolve) and **gc** (drop unreferenced pins, dead workspaces' branches) |
| `jj squash --into main` | **promote**: move each system's base branch to the fork -- fast-forward if the base is unchanged since the fork point, native merge where one exists, refuse otherwise |
| `jj abandon` / `jj squash` | the VCS's own; what history no longer names, `gc` releases |
| `jj op log` / `jj undo` | **ops** / **undo**: tether's own log of what each command did to the stores, and the reversal of an entry where the store still allows it; **repair** rebuilds what a manifest promises |
| -- | **export** / **publish** (history as SQL tables) and **import** (the object set from a registry query) |

## State, pin, fork

For each object a backend implements three things, in increasing order of what
the system must support:

- **State**: what the object *is* right now -- an Icechunk `snapshot_id`, a
  Neon `(lsn, next_xid, branch)`, a Delta `version`, a directory's size/mtime
  digest.
  Comparing states is how drift is detected without watching anything.
- **Pin**: a durable, GC-proof native reference to a state, named
  `tether.<pin_id>` -- an Icechunk tag, a protected Neon child branch, a git
  tag, a Lance tag, a Dolt tag. `pin_id = <dataset-id>.<blake2b(kind, locator
  identity, content state)[:16]>`, so identical state on the same object yields
  the same pin within a dataset and re-committing an unchanged object is a
  no-op. The dataset id in front is the [namespace](#namespaces).
- **Fork**: a fresh writable branch created off a pin -- or, for objects with
  `pin = "record"`, straight off the recorded state, skipping the native ref
  entirely. `tether new` decides one per Forkable object, named
  `tether.ws.<dataset-id>.<workspace-id>.<key-slug>-<key-hash>`, so neither
  datasets, workspaces, nor look-alike keys collide, and by default
  creates it lazily on the first writable `open` (pins are durable, so the
  branch can wait; pin-less objects fork immediately because their recorded
  state cannot wait). `--eager` creates them all during `new`.

## Namespaces

`tether.toml` carries an 8-hex `[dataset] id`, generated by `init` and
committed, so every clone of the dataset shares it. Every native ref tether
creates starts with it: pins are `tether.<id>.<hash>`, working branches
`tether.ws.<id>.<workspace>.<key>`. `gc` only ever considers refs in its own
namespace -- several datasets can pin the same Icechunk repo or Neon project
and none of them can delete another's pins or branches, `--force-prune`
included; foreign refs are counted in the plan's notes and left alone. The
price is that the same content pinned by two datasets is two refs.

## Plans

Every command that writes to an external system (`commit` pins, `new` forks,
`gc` unpins and deletes branches, `promote`, `import`, `repair`) is a
read-only **plan** followed by an **apply**. `--dry-run` prints the plan,
`--plan FILE` saves it, `--from-plan FILE` applies it later; apply re-checks
that states and manifests still match what the plan recorded and refuses
otherwise (`StalePlanError`). The Python API exposes the same pairs:
`plan_commit`/`apply_commit`, `plan_new`/`apply_new`, `plan_gc`/`apply_gc`,
and so on.

## The operation log

The VCS records the manifests. It cannot see which native refs `commit`
created, which branches `new` forked or reset and what their heads were
before, what `gc` deleted, or where `promote` moved a base branch from. Every
apply therefore appends an entry to `.tether/ops.jsonl` -- per workspace,
untracked, append-only, like jj's own `op log` -- holding the plan it applied,
what it did, and what it replaced. `tether ops` lists it.

`tether undo [ID]` reverses an entry *where the store still allows it* and
says exactly what it could not reverse:

| Undoing a ... | does |
| --- | --- |
| `commit` | uncommits it (the manifests become working-tree changes again; the pins stay, still referenced) while it is still the working copy's parent |
| `new` / a lazy fork | deletes the branches it created, re-points the ones it reset to their recorded heads, restores `workspace.toml`, returns the VCS working copy if it has not moved since |
| `gc` | recreates deleted branches from their recorded heads and listings from the VCS; deleted **pins are irreversible** -- once a manifest references them again, `repair` recreates them while the state is still reachable |
| `import` / `add` / `remove` | restores the manifests |
| `promote` | is refused, with the previous base heads printed for a manual reset; backends only fast-forward |

A branch that gained writes since the operation is never deleted or reset
silently: `undo` refuses until you commit them or pass `--discard`. The same
rule applies to `new` itself -- a working branch holding writes you never
committed is only reset with `--discard`.

`tether repair` is the other direction: given the manifests, rebuild what they
promise. A pin whose native ref is gone is recreated from the recorded state
(as long as the store still has it); a working branch this workspace expects
but the store lost is forked again. `--all-history` checks every commit's pins.

What `jj undo` / `git reset` can and cannot do is unchanged by all this: they
revert the manifests, never the stores. Use them for the VCS side, `tether
undo` for tether's.

## Capability tiers

Backends declare capabilities; commands degrade explicitly by tier.

- **Observed** (`FINGERPRINT`): drift detection only. `commit` records the state
  and marks it `recoverable = false`. A local directory by mtime, an
  unversioned S3 prefix.
- **Addressable** (`+ ADDRESSABLE`): the recorded state can be read back later
  with nothing to create or GC. An S3 object in a versioned bucket, a Delta
  version, a DuckLake snapshot.
- **Pinnable** (`+ PIN`): a durable native ref can be created and deleted;
  `verify` and `gc` apply.
- **Forkable** (`+ FORK`): a writable branch can be created off a pin; `new`
  forks and `open` returns a writable handle. Icechunk, Neon, Iceberg, Lance,
  lakeFS, Dolt, git/jj.

Orthogonal flags refine behavior: `CHEAP_FINGERPRINT` (metadata only),
`RETENTION_BOUND` (recoverability expires with a retention window),
`NEEDS_QUIESCENCE` (commit checks for active writers), `ATOMIC_REF`
(create-if-absent pins), `DIFF` (native content diffs), `HISTORY` (native
log), `BRANCH_IS_STORAGE` (deleting a branch reclaims its data; `gc` never
prunes such a branch without force), `PROMOTE` (fast-forward the base branch
to a fork) and `MERGE` (three-way merge a fork into the base).

## Handles, not data

tether is never in the data path. `open` returns a typed handle carrying the
native address -- an Icechunk session on the right branch or tag, a Postgres
URL, a `DeltaTable` at a version, a `lakefs://repo/ref/prefix/` URI -- and steps
aside. You read and write with the system's own library.

## Stale working copies

For every working ref, the workspace remembers the committed state it was
forked from (or last committed at by this workspace). If that object's
manifest now records a different state -- a teammate committed, or you `jj
new`'d to another revision -- the fork no longer starts where the dataset says
it does: that object is *stale*. `status` names the stale objects and writable
`open` refuses with `StaleWorkingCopyError` until you `tether new` again. It is
per object and per workspace: your own commits never make you stale,
registering or removing *other* objects changes nothing, and `track` objects
(which write to the base branch) are never stale. This is jj's
stale-working-copy check applied to external branches.

## Content and address

A state is a small dict, but its keys do two different jobs. *Content* keys
say what the data is (an Icechunk snapshot id, a Neon `next_xid`, a git sha).
*Address* keys say where to find or cut it and can move without the data
changing: Neon's `lsn` advances on checkpoints, git's `change_id` exists only
when jj is installed. Backends declare the address keys as `VOLATILE_KEYS`;
drift detection, the unchanged check in `commit`, pin ids, listing names, and
`promote`'s comparisons use only the content, while `open`, `pin`, and
`verify` get the whole state. Iceberg's `metadata_location`, which changes on
every table commit on any branch, is not in the state at all.

## Drift

Snapshots happen on every command, so drift is caught at the next touch rather
than by a daemon. An Observed object registered as immutable (the default for
`file`) that changes on disk is an *error* at `status`; a Forkable object whose
working branch moved is simply `modified` and will be pinned on the next
commit. `verify` answers the other question -- do the pins we recorded still
resolve to the states we recorded? -- cheaply by default, deeply with `--deep`,
and across every commit with `--all-history`.

## Listings

A directory or prefix state is only a digest, so it cannot be diffed on its
own. At commit time the `file` backend hands tether a per-file listing, stored
content-addressed under `.tether/listings/` and committed with the manifests
(the same trick as DVC's `.dir` files). `diff --content` compares two listings
file by file; `gc` prunes listings no manifest references.

## What tether does not do

- Cross-system atomicity. A commit records each object's state within a
  capture window; point-consistency requires quiesced writers.
- Reimplement history, branching, or sharing. That is the VCS's job. tether's
  own `undo` covers only what tether did to the stores.
- Queries or transactions across systems.
